subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO AMENDMENT OF PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government legislation on prescription drug patent is a good example of the definition of Canada's Conservatives.
The only consequence this policy can have is higher drug prices. It is a policy which compromises the access to and availability of prescription drugs. It is a policy which helps the major American multinationals. It is a policy which flies in the face of the Canadian progressive health care system established by Liberal Governments. It is a policy which Canadians reject outright.
I urge the Government to stop forcing Canadians to pay higher drug prices, to withdraw the Bill, and to be sensitive and fair to Canadians who need these drugs. We must make every effort to improve their standard of living instead of debasing their integrity and their existence.

subsubtopic: U.S.S.R.-JEWISH CITIZENS-PROMISE OF PERMISSION TO EMIGRATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a new but significant promise from the Kremlin to permit 11,000 Jewish refusniks to emigrate to Israel this year was reported yesterday. They are all on a long standing list of cases presented to the Soviets at the Reykjavik summit.
All of these people have been denied for a very long time the most basic human right, freedom to choose to leave the Soviet Union. We applaud Mr. Edward Bronfman and Mr. Abram of the United States for their efforts in negotiating this promise of the release of 11,000 people. I cannot applaud the U.S.S.R. for a promise, but we are encouraged. We will applaud the U.S.S.R. when they grant all the basic human rights to their citizens, including the right to pursue their religious convictions in the Soviet Union.
This latest promise is a perfect occasion to put the alleged policy of openness, or "glasnost", to the litmus test.

subsubtopic: PROPERTY DAMAGE CAUSED BY TWIN TRACKING PROJECT IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has now been many weeks since the National Research Council submitted its report on the damage done to private property as the result of the Canadian National twin tracking project in Kamloops and Rayleigh, British Columbia. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) waited for the receipt of this report before taking action with CN with respect to compensating those whose homes and businesses have experienced structural damage, and before requiring CN to take corrective action to eliminate future damage.
The people of Kamloops and Rayleigh have been very patient. They have waited for months as studies have been conducted while watching cracks in their walls widen, foundations crumbling, and water lines break. CN has not been especially co-operative in recognizing the problem, and providing compensation or taking any corrective action.
Leadership by the Minister of Transport and the federal Government is now necessary. I urge the Minister to take action now to ensure that those who suffered, through no fault of their own, as a result of CN's twin tracking program through residential areas, are treated fairly by the railway which is itself the ultimate responsibility of the federal Government.

April 1, 1987

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO SMALL OIL PRODUCING COMPANIES-IMPACT ON ECONOMY OF ALBERTA
GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO SMALL OIL PRODUCING COMPANIES-IMPACT ON ECONOMY OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ottawa's $350 million a year offer to the oil industry might signal the beginning of annual investments of $1 billion in exploration for and development of untapped reserves in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The National Energy Program had seriously distorted the industry, and it was up to the Government to make sure that small companies, one of the most important elements of the industry, would survive.
As a matter of fact, small companies had not been on the receiving end of the NEP bonanza to the same extent as major concerns, and their efforts to develop traditional western reserves had even been thwarted. Such assistance to small oil producers will boost the Albertan economy at a time when future prospects do not look very promising. It is aimed at a sector from which Alberta's economy draws its strength and on which rests the future of the province.
The help offered by the Government of Ottawa to small producers will enable that industry to rally and survive while waiting for renewed wider scale exploration boosted by higher world prices.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) was right, and Ottawa makes it possible for Alberta to get through the doldrums and save the jobs of skilled workers.

Mr. Speaker, 300 political prisoners in Chile have been on a hunger strike since February 25, 1987, in protest against unfair trials and treatment. The hunger strike started in connection with two trials involving members of an armed opposition group who are accused of smuggling arms into the country, and persons accused of attempting to kill General Pinochet. In both of these cases prisoners were badly tortured, a fact which has been documented by America's Watch, an American human rights organization.
This organization has interviewed 17 people who are detained. The interviews include reports that rats were let loose on victims' faces. Prisoners also received the normal application of electric shock to the most sensitive parts of the body. Some of the prisoners were also submerged in water to
the point of losing consciousness, badly beaten, and sexually abused.
The hunger strikers are demanding the release of all political prisoners through an amnesty or else be allowed to exchange their sentence for exile, and the end to political appointments of special military prosecutors to deal with particular cases and the transfer of judicial proceedings from military to civilian courts.
Amnesty International has asked that urgent action be taken. I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to condemn the Chilean Government for its gross indecent violation of human rights and to urge that Government to meet the requests of the political prisoners.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT SPONSORED ADVERTISING CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tourism is the fifth largest industry in Canada and is growing every year. Our Government has recently increased its tourism advertising by $5.5 million to attract more visitors from the United States. This will help Canada maintain its momentum of last year when a record number of Americans spent their vacations in Canada. The additional funding will be spent on expanded television and magazine advertising under the award winning theme of "Canada: The World Next Door".
The tourism industry is vital to Canada. It employs more than 600,000 Canadians and generates $20 billion in receipts. In Alberta tourism is the third largest industry and we are working hard to ensure that it continues its strong and healthy growth. It is a key factor in our desire to diversify our economy, and is an integral part of our future. Tourism is vital to our Government's economical renewal and we should all make an effort to ensure that Canada is indeed "the world next door".

Mr. Speaker, seniors, single parents and other Canadians with low incomes are fuming at the Tory Government for the amount of personal income tax they are having to pay for 1986. I would like to read one of several letters from my constituents on this matter.
Dear, Mr. Parry:
My mother had a total income of $9,885.60 last year. I calculated her
income tax for her and she owes $236.20.
April 1, 1987

Mr. Parry, my mother is in her 70s, her only income is through pensions. It does not seem right that she should have to pay tax at all. Also, her taxes to the Town are due this month, she has no idea where to get the money from ... Why are the poor being penalized again?
I should cite the figures calculated by Mr. Murray Kelso of Fort Frances. Someone who paid no federal tax in 1985 on $1,430 of taxable income has to pay $99 in 1986; and on $3,000 someone who had to pay $254 of federal tax in 1985 has to pay $352 in 1986.
A single parent writes me:
Financially, I would have been better to have stayed home with my children; between saving child care expenses and having a larger income return. My situation is not uncommon.
Indeed, these impositions on low-income Canadians cry out for a remedy.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday this Government and the Government of Quebec decided to invest $220 million, that is $110 million each, in the General Motors factory at Sainte-Therese. At stake are 5,500 jobs in Quebec and 5,400 jobs in Ontario, especially in Oshawa. The Leader of the NDP, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), did nothing in this respect to help his constituents. He was and still is against helping the private sector.
Although the Leader of the NDP accepts source deductions from Canadian workers and also benefits from our job creating activities, as the Member for Oshawa he has remained silent and very negative about an issue that involves Quebec and his own riding. Workers in Oshawa know this and will not forget! When will the Leader of the NDP show his true colours, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: DECAY OF MAPLE TREES-REQUEST FOR CONCERTED CANADA-UNITED STATES ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not long ago, the President of the UPA wrote a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in which he said, and I quote: Our maples, the symbol of Canada, are dying.
Mr. Speaker, the UPA wanted to make the leader of this Government aware of the fact that one of the worst disasters in the history of Canadian agriculture may compromise the growth and survival of the maple syrup industry. The deterioration of our maple trees has been increasing and spreading
ever since the first cases were identified in 1979-80. According to the findings of recent studies carried out by the Quebec Department of Energy and Resources, 85 per cent of Quebec maple stands are now showing signs of deterioration, varying from slight to very serious.
It is imperative that the Canadian Government put pressure on the Americans to agree to a definite program, so that we can stop the deterioration process, stop pollution and get rid of the sources of pollution.

Mr. Speaker, tonight Canadians of Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian origin, as well as their friends and supporters, will gather on Parliament Hill to celebrate the fifteenth annual Baltic Evening. Baltic Canadians have a special understanding and appreciation of the good fortune Canadians enjoy living in a free and democratic nation. Baltic independence was lost when the Soviet Union forcibly occupied the Baltic States. This occasion serves as a reminder of the need to protect and encourage the spirit of freedom wherever it is found.
The Baltic culture has flourished in Canada, and Canadians of Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian heritage have proudly contributed their strengths and perseverance to Canada, and the cause of freedom. I call on all Members of the House to join Canada's Baltic community in celebrating this special occasion, and by their participation and presence to recognize the tremendous contribution the Baltic communities have made to the growth and development of Canada, and to demonstrate that Canada does not and will not accept the forcible and illegal occupation of the Baltic States by the Soviet Union.

Mr. Speaker, an 11-year-old constituent of mine wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last week as follows:
We, the students of Claude E. Garton School, Thunder Bay, Ontario, feel that charging taxes on popsicles, ice cream and other snacks is unfair to the children. We work hard selling newspapers, babysitting, shovelling snow, household chores, etc. This money pays for snacks, fads and fashions, etc. that we want, but if you take more money from us there will be no reason to work since you will be taking money from our pockets too.
We appeal to you to kindly change this law.

April 1, 1987
This letter was supported by several hundred of her classmates and friends.
This letter, Mr. Speaker, makes a very important point about the effect that excessive taxation has on Canadians. The Conference Board of Canada made a further point about high taxation last week when it pointed out that the economy is slowing down because the federal Government is taking too much in taxes. Disposable income is stagnating, rather than rising.
I join, Mr. Speaker, with the children of Claude E. Garton School in calling on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) not to tax the snacks that the children want to enjoy.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the House to an editorial in today's Ottawa Citizen regarding the report of the Special Committee on Child Care. In that editorial the statement is made, and I quote:
A good day-care centre can cost $10,000 a year or more for each child.
We have all heard the claim, Mr. Speaker, that day care workers are underpaid and that wages account for 80 per cent of child care costs.
I have been informed that the accepted care-giver to child ratio for preschool children-and by that I mean children ages three to five-is one care-giver to eight children.
Using simple arithmetic, if the cost per child is $10,000 a year and 80 per cent of that $10,000 goes to wages, as is claimed, the care-givers should each be receiving $64,000 a year in wages.
Today is April Fool's Day, Mr. Speaker, but in the important matter of dealing with the future of our children I believe we should stop fooling around and start providing the Canadian people with the facts, the facts that add up.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SITUATION OF SHIPYARD WORKERS IN LEVIS, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian shipyards especially in Quebec are in a
major crisis situation. When I saw the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) rising a while ago, I thought that he was going to stand up and fight for the workers in his riding, more specifically the 2,300 Levis shipyard workers who were counting on him for help.
Last Friday, Mr. Speaker, when I was in the Quebec area I took pictures of the shipyard to show just how idle and empty it is. There is not a single ship nor a single worker in the shipyard. On three different occasions, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) did promise to build the Caribou there. Well, once again he has misled the Levis people, the Quebec people, for the Caribou venture has been delayed.
I dare hope that the next time the Hon. Member for Levis rises in the House, it will be to stand up for his constituents.

subsubtopic: UKRAINE-HARASSMENT OF CHRISTIAN BELIEVERS BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I stand before this House to speak out on behalf of victims of religious repression by Soviet authorities, and specifically the continued harassment and imprisonment of individuals seeking to keep alive the spirit of Christianity in Ukraine.
In 1975 Vasyl Kobryn was dismissed from his job for refusing to work on Easter Sunday, which had been declared a workday in order to harass Christian believers working at the factory. Kobryn lodged complaints and signed statements regarding his treatment, eventually becoming an active member of the Group for the Defence of Believer's Rights and the Rights of the Church in Ukraine, rising to the position of chairman in 1983.
As a result of his activities Kobryn was arrested as a criminal, tried and convicted of spreading so-called lies against the Soviet system.
The Soviet Government continues to take direct action against individuals whose faith and belief in Christianity have led them to take a stand against those forces who would deny them the basic right to practise their religious beliefs openly.
Once more I must urge the Canadian Government to seek effective means to impress upon the Soviet Government our strong and united opposition to this continued persecution.
April 1, 1987

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER LINGUISTIC DUALITY IS PROTECTED IN FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his report tabled yesterday, the Commissioner of Official Languages criticized the Government for its inertia and made it abundantly clear that in this area as in so many others, the Conservative Government is serving up a lot of promises and hollow phrases but very little action.
We all know that bilingualism is one of the vital elements that distinguishes Canadians from Americans. Could the Prime Minister give the House the assurance he will protect our linguistic duality in his free trade negotiations with the United States?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER LINGUISTIC DUALITY IS PROTECTED IN FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Commissioner commented favourably on several federal initiatives with respect to bilingualism. For all of us it is the cornerstone of our life as a nation and as a people, and there will be new projects that will provide even more support for this Canadian reality.
As far as linguistic duality is concerned, I think I mentioned the subject in my speech on September 25, 1985, here in the House, and during the debate where we said quite clearly that this language dimension was not only enriching but indispensable for Canada's future and that our cultural and linguistic life was not on the table in negotiations that were strictly concerned with trade.

subtopic: COMMISSIONER'S REFERENCE TO CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: What concrete steps is the Prime Minister taking in supervising our negotiations with the United States on free trade to ensure that our bilingualism and our policy of multiculturalism are not being endangered by the style of those negotiations?

subtopic: COMMISSIONER'S REFERENCE TO CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted-and I will wait for the "blues"-that the Leader of the Opposition says that in this report the Commissioner of Official Languages expresses concern that we are going "to sell out our two official languages" in free trade negotiations. I am going to read the report again very carefully, because that strikes me as being a very grave distortion of what the Commissioner for Official Languages said. I will read it carefully, and I urge the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to do the same.
The Commissioner expresses concerns to which he is entitled. It is his job to protect official languages in the country, and we give him every support and every encouragement in that endeavour. However, I think I made very clear on behalf of the Government on September 25 at the University of Chicago, in a major speech on behalf of the Government of Canada, and here in the House of Commons during the debate on free trade, that culture and language were very much cornerstones of our national identity, that they were not at any time or in any circumstance in jeopardy or part of the negotiation process. That has been accepted by all sides. That has been accepted by the Americans. That has been accepted by all reasonable Canadians, and I hope eventually to persuade the Leader of the Opposition.

subtopic: COMMISSIONER'S REFERENCE TO CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: I think the Prime Minister ought to begin by attempting to persuade the Commissioner of Official Languages.

Mr. Speaker, my last question is directed to the Minister of State (Privatization).
In his report, the Commissioner of Official Languages says, and I quote, that "the privatization of federal agencies should be carefully scrutinised from the language angle to forestall any slippage in bilingual performance. As this subject is becoming more and more topical, we badly need a legal guideline to protect service to the public."

April 1, 1987

Could the Minister inform the House today what steps she has taken to guarantee that in selling our Crown corporations, we are not selling out bilingualism?

In the Teleglobe case, the headquarters of the company will remain in Montreal. In all our companies which are under review, this is an issue we are addressing very carefully.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-COMPLIANCE WITH LINGUISTIC REQUIREMENTS BY DEPUTY MINISTERS

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-COMPLIANCE WITH LINGUISTIC REQUIREMENTS BY DEPUTY MINISTERS

There has been no Government decision which could weaken the efforts of this
Government as concerns official languages.
In light of this assurance, can the Minister confirm a report carried by the Official Language Commissioner's report yesterday, which is in The Globe and Mail this morning, that a recent government decision has made it easier for Deputy Ministers and senior managers to avoid complying with the linguistic requirements for their positions?
[ Translation]

speechtext: In response to my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier, Mr. Speaker, I can say that the Government is as committed as ever in its pursuit of linguistic duality in Canada, as it has always been. Mr. Speaker, I can also say that ours is the Government which, under the leadership of our Prime Minister of course, has formally promised to introduce the first and greatly overdue amendments to a statute which has been on the books for 16 or 17 years already. These amendments will be introduced in the House in the next few weeks or months so that the legislation be more attuned to the current needs of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, this Minister issued the guidelines I have here-I can send him a copy if he does not have one-to reduce the linguistic requirements for appointments of deputy ministers in the national capital regional and to the EX management group bilingual positions in a bilingual region.
Knowing the impact and influence which a unilingual superior may have on employees, on his own staff, when it comes to the language of work, how can the Minister explain that these policy statements which originate from his Department, such retrograde statements of management policy
coming from him and his officials, indicate obvious and terribly retrograde laxity with respect to leadership within the Public Service of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with respect to the languages of work, the only laxity to which we can indeed point a finger is the laxity of the former Government. The new Government has taken and is taking steps to review the legislation and regulations as a whole to make sure that the public is getting better services in both official languages, and that the language of work is improved in both official languages. This is what we are doing, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In the area of child care, the greatest need now, all experts agree, is for increased services. But in the Minister's Budget, $300 million have not yet been allocated. Why does not the Minister use this money to increase these services right away?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this question has been answered before, namely, when the Minister of Finance came forward with his Budget in February. A direct decision was taken that decisions such as child care would be made and announced by the Government as an individual policy item. The Minister of Finance also indicated in his Budget that there were designated figures in it. Perhaps the Hon. Member could read them. As I pointed out before, that was the approach we took. Nothing has changed from when I gave him the answer the last time.

Mr. Speaker, what has changed is that we have had a report brought in by a committee of this House supported only by a majority of Conservative Members on the problem of day care. Recommendations have been made that are absolutely disastrous in terms of meeting the need for services. The Government of Prince Edward Island joined this morning with the Government of the Province of Ontario, the Government of Nova Scotia, the Government of Manitoba, all other experts in the field and church leaders in saying that the priority recommendations of the Conservative committee were wrong. As well, they have called for an immediate increase in services in terms of daycare places for the children of Canada. Will the Minister now make a decision, change those priorities and use the $300 million to provide the badly needed services for children?
April 1, 1987

The Minister has talked about choice. As far as I understand it, one thing all Parties agree on is that there should be a great choice for families in day-care services. Considering that some 75 per cent of Canadians say that the immediate priority is to have an increase in services, why does the Government not do something about that and allocate money that would increase services for the children of Canada who need them?

subsubtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-PARTICIPATION OF FRANCOPHONES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and concerns the Government's apparent lack of commitment to bilingualism. As the Prime Minister knows, there is a proposal before the Treasury Board which would reduce Francophone participation objectives in the RCMP. The Official Languages Commissioner was extremely critical of this action, stating that it would dangerously compromise the force's ability to meet the requirements of the Official Languages Act and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If the Prime Minister is as committed as he says he is to bilingualism in Canada, will he instruct the RCMP that this Parliament will not tolerate reductions in Francophone participation levels in the RCMP?

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Finance. Following the unanimous report of this House on credit cards that was tabled in this House, the Minister of State said that if rates did not come down, Parliament would act.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister also stated that the Government policy would be to have credit card interest rates that would not be higher than 5 per cent over prime. My question to the Minister of State for Finance is this: Is it still this Government's policy to have credit card interest rates that are no higher than 5 per cent over prime?

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member asked that question. It allows me to clarify two important mistakes made in his question. First, I made it very clear that, in my mind, interest rates are too high. The way to bring those rates down is to have the market-place do it. Parliament's action in this realm does not necessarily have to be action on rates. It can be on disclosure. It can be on all sorts of dimensions of the problem, perhaps including rates.
Second, the committee report and the research that went into it mentioned the 4 per cent or 5 per cent above prime rate profit margin. I have said that I am looking at that as perhaps a guideline. Whether that is the proper profit or not would depend on the type of card and the type of enterprise.

In a press conference the Minister suggested that card issuers should charge 4 per cent or 5 per cent above the prime rate. I was just quoting his own words.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. It concerns the decision not to allow Telefilm Canada to keep $18.5 million and let it be rolled over into the next fiscal year from the past year's funding. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe that is exactly the kind of policy we are pursuing. If the Hon. Member had cared to look at the record she would have seen that initially Telefilm Canada was funded under a long-term program which was converted to meet the actual annual cash flow needs of Telefilm Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was shouted down by members of the New Democratic Party as I tried to put some facts on record regarding how Canadians feel about Bill C-22 and its intent and purpose which is to restore patent protection for creators of new drugs and to promote research and development in Canada along with better health care.
A public opinion survey was undertaken and the following statement was put to the people of Canada for response: "If I have to choose between lower prices for today's drugs or higher prices with more research money spent to speed up the development of new treatments, I would rather pay higher prices". In other words, people were asked if they would rather pay higher prices in order to have more research and development. It was a very loaded question. The choice is higher prices or lower prices but with higher prices there will be research and development and a search for new treatments. Twenty-eight per cent of the respondents disagreed with that statement. They said that they did not want higher prices, they wanted lower prices.
Amazing on such a loaded question.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
A loaded question? We are asking people if they want higher prices and the Hon. Member is asking if that is a loaded question in favour of the NDP argument. Sixty-four per cent of Canadians who responded to the survey agree with that position. They agree that what we are doing is right. Sixty-four per cent agree that research and development is the most important question.
Another statement made by the survey for response was: "I would support the Bill if the Government put in place a way of

April 1, 1987
Patent Act
making sure that drug price increases would not be higher than the rate of inflation". That is precisely what is contained in the Bill. Increases in drug prices will not be higher than the rate of inflation. What did Canadians think of that statement? Eighty-two per cent of them agreed with that provision in this Bill. Six per cent said that it would depend, and those must be the Liberals. Twelve per cent disagreed, and those must be the New Democrats.
For days on end we have heard petitions and claims of outrage around the country about the provisions of Bill C-22. We can see now from these questions asked of Canadians that in fact all of those charges and claims are nonsense. If the opposition Parties believe, as they seem to believe because of statements they have made, that the will of the people is what should drive us, they should support this Bill. If they believe that more research and development in this important area is important, they should support it. If they believe that the inventor who has created something of value deserves patent protection, just as any creator, they should support it. If they think Canada has a responsibility in the world to do its share of research and development in the search for cures for Alzheimer's, for cancer, for multiple sclerosis and for other afflictions, and if they think Canada should be a first-rate country participating in this important area as a first-rate country, they should support this legislation. If they believe that they have a responsibility to do what is best for Canada, they should support this legislation.
It is only small minds and narrow partisan purposes that keep opposition Members resorting to cheap parliamentary devices to delay even a discussion in the House of this legislation. It is a pathetic Opposition. I hope they will soon come to their senses. I hope we can pass this Bill so that Canadian scientists and university graduates will know that they will have an opportunity to work in Canada in the search for cures for these diseases and will not have to continue to go to the United States or Europe to pursue their careers. I think the public has spoken, and it is about time the House listened and acted.

Mr. Speaker, the poll the Minister had conducted is very interesting. To say it is slanted would be putting it mildly. I cannot imagine any poll with results like that unless the test group were known supporters of the legislation. Even 20 per cent of those initially in favour of the legislation would have changed their mind by the time they were called. The poll runs directly contrary to one published in the Reid report of January 1, 1987. It said that 58 per cent of Canadians oppose the Bill and only 30 per cent support it. Some 12 per cent are unsure. There is a significant level of opposition among Canadians from all walks of life. It is not just one particular group.
Information released with the poll states that most Canadians expect the proposed legislation will result in increased profits for the drug companies rather than more research and
development activity in Canada. It says that perception is very widespread across various population groupings, including current federal Conservative supporters. Even the Government's own supporters are opposed to the legislation. We have stated in this House that all Canadians are opposed to this legislation and accentuated the opposition of the young, the sick and the elderly. However, the poll indicates all Canadians oppose the legislation.
The information supplied with the poll goes on to say most consumers expect drug prices will increase as a result of the legislation. Even supporters of the initiative expect it to result in increased prices. Who is left? I suggest it is the Minister and maybe two or three members of his caucus who may really believe this legislation will do some good.
It is incredible that we are even debating legislation which is so harmful to the people of this country. It is incredible that the Government has not woken up to the fact that Canadians are opposed to the Bill. Everyone knows the Government has been solicited by the U.S. drug lobby. They have gone to members of the Government and people in our embassy in the U.S. They have used every possible trick in the book. They have used influential lobbyists with connections to the Government. It is rank, to say the least, that the people who elected the Government with an overwhelming majority now find that support thrown back in their face. Their feelings concerning drug prices are being completely ignored.
I want to compliment my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), for the job he has done in putting forward the position of this Party on the legislation. Having done that, I would like to deal particularly with the proposed amendment which relates to inserting in the legislation a definition of research.
We have been told that if this Bill is passed the drug companies will invest $1.4 billion in research and development in Canada. The Minister has gone across the country telling everyone that they are in line for research and development money. He has been like a Tory Johnny Appleseed going from region to region telling people that their ship has come in. Those areas are experiencing regional disparity, they need industry, and he has held out the hope to them that he has the answer. All they have to do is have faith in the legislation and they will be the beneficiaries of a brand new industry employing numerous people. That is a fallacy, to put it mildly. It has built up the hopes of a great many people, but the people are not taken in. They do not believe for one minute that this legislation will mean additional jobs. The Government says that 3,000 good high-paying jobs will be created. The facts tell us differently.
Before 1969, when the former Liberal Government brought in legislation to reduce the rampant rip-off of consumers by the major drug companies, there was no investment in research and development in Canada. In fact, there has been considerable investment since that time and it has nothing to do with this legislation. Where in the legislation are we shown what will happen if the drug companies do not give us the research
April 1, 1987

and development they say they will? What are we going to do? We have a parliamentary review but there is no linkage. Who in the heck do we expect will believe what the Government is saying? It is incredible. Not only will it increase drug prices but it insults the intelligence of Canadians.
The legislation would require the multinationals to make or buy their basic ingredients in Canada if they want full patent protection. The new legislation removes that requirement. We are regressing. There is nothing here for the people to believe in. When the Government, through its own ineptitude, was unable to introduce the Bill in June, instead of apologizing or feeling embarrassed it punished Canadians by making the Bill even more ridiculous than it was then.
The Government says that over the next 10 years we are going to get $1.4 billion in research and development. That is absolutely incredible. Multinationals will have their profits rise by $3.5 billion over the next five years. The problem is that even if they did invest $1.4 billion in R and D, that is considerably less than the $4 billion to $5 billion it will cost Canadians through increased drug prices. There is no way the people of this country can win. The question really comes down to what will be the most damaging medicine to Canadians, and excuse the pun. We know that regardless of what happens it will not be in the interests of the people of this country.
I hope, I think in vain, that the Government will withdraw this Draconian legislation. The rest of the western countries look upon what Canada has done concerning competition in the distribution of drugs as a model. We are now going in reverse by throwing this model legislation and an enviable position away, and with it the price stability of drugs in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in the debate on this amendment to Bill C-22. The Opposition is asking the Government to include a definition of research and development in its legislation because we do not trust the multinational drug companies, we do not trust the Government, and we do not trust the Minister.
This legislation will result in a substantial increase in price for new drugs. It is estimated that Canadians saved over $200 million in 1983 because of the existing restriction in the amount of time the multinationals could have a monopoly in marketing their drugs. The Government has told us that this legislation is necessary in order to encourage more research and development in this country. In fact, the Minister stated that it will create over 3,000 new high-tech research jobs in Canada. Documents obtained through access to information show that the Minister's Department has other figures. While the Minister claims that 3,000 new high-quality research jobs will be created, his departmental document shows that in the best case scenario there will only be 1,148 new jobs. The document also shows that another 652 jobs are classified as technical, meaning lab technician jobs which could be filled by those with an undergraduate or community college standing.
Patent Act
According to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, another 620 jobs would be for managers, cleaners, animal keepers, statisticians and clerks.
Instead of the 3,000 high-quality research jobs for Canadian scientists and biochemists in the next 10 years, as the Minister has claimed, his Department shows in its study that there will only be 1,148 jobs. That is why we do not trust the Government, the Minister and certainly not the multinational corporations. We are asking for a definition of research in the legislation to which the drug companies would have to adhere. Why is the Government opposed to including such a definition in the legislation? Why does it want the Cabinet and the bureaucrats to decide what research means? It is not even willing to include the definition of research as it is found in the Income Tax Act. The broad term of research can include many things.
When the committee of the House was dealing with this legislation it heard testimony that the type of research that occurs in this country is often low-grade research, done to ensure that the product the multinational is developing in this country meets the standards of the Department of Health and Welfare. It is also research conducted to develop variations of existing drugs due to the high profit margin on these drugs; the drug companies are attempting to develop variations of those drugs.
For example, Doctor Lexchin, who is a leading authority in this country on the economics of the drug industry and the type of research it does, has stated:
So the pattern of drug company reinvestment in research and development worldwide tends to be that they go for the bucks; they do not go for the health needs.
Later in his comments he stated:
Without specifying what kind of research the government wants these multinationals to engage in, it is our feeling that the pattern of investment here in Canada, whatever new money we get, will be the same as the pattern of investment worldwide. In other words, most of the products that are researched here will have no major therapeutic value.
Yet the Minister stood in the House recently to insinuate that without this type of legislation we will not see the cures for Alzheimer's disease or cancer or other diseases for which men and women throughout the world are trying to find cures. The Minister is suggesting that this Bill is necessary because the drug companies need the money to develop cures that we all hope will be found. However, we do not know that this Bill will be of any assistance in developing cures to these ailments because there is no guarantee that the billions of dollars the multinational companies will derive as a result of the Bill will be spent in developing cures for such diseases as Alzheimer's and cancer. We do not trust the Government. That is why we ask that it include a definition of research in the legislation.
During his remarks this afternoon the Minister commented on the poll results. 1 have the results of two independent polls that were conducted by Angus Reid and Gallup. Both polls show that an overwhelming majority of Canadians are opposed to this legislation. The drug industry, ever mindful of its image

and always having the resources to work on it, bought its own poll. It is not surprising that the results seem to show that the majority of Canadians are behind the Government's legislation in Bill C-22. It is very interesting that two independent polls- Gallup and Reid-show one thing while the one commissioned by the multinational drug companies seems to show something else. The Government, the drug industry, and the Minister in particular have a credibility problem. They are not believed by the people of this country. The people of this country do not believe that that Minister is acting in the interests of the Canadian people. They believe, and I support them in their belief, that the Minister and the Government are acting in the interests of the multinational corporations. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is a branch plant manager and that is all he is. He is attempting to run this country as a branch plant. I think the Canadian people feel enough is enough and are just hoping for an election which will turf this Government out so we can have a Government by Canadians and for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment to Bill C-22 which is before the House today is, I think, completely agreeable to the Government. The Government has not bothered to have the Minister in the House for the debate, but since the Minister is basing his reason for this legislation on the fact that he is going to gain a lot of extra research and development-he talks about $1.4 billion of research and development-he would want to identify what "research" means. The motion before us defines research in the following way:
""research is exploratory and innovative work undertaken on a systematic basis towards the acquisition of new knowledge in new ways. New knowledge involves the integration of newly acquired information into existing hypothesis, the formulation and testing of new hypothesis or the re-evaluation of existing observations;".
That is not something the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) dreamed up on his own, although he is certainly capable of developing a definition, having a legal mind and an excellent legal background. He has taken this definition directly from Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Act, which defines research and development. Therefore, I think this is a valid description.
The Government does not want to say it is bringing in this legislation to pay billions of dollars back to the multinational corporations in the United States because the President of the United States twisted the Prime Minister's arm. But there has to be some reason for the Government bringing forward this legislation, and that is, we will gain research and development and $1.4 billion of investment.
It is well documented that for every $1 billion of R and D the Government gains, Canadians will have to pay $3 billion $4 billion in additional drug costs. So who wins? The multinationals win. Canadians will not win because they must pay.
Members of the House of Commons will not pay because they have a drug plan. It is not 100 per cent but it covers most of their drugs. It will not be the people in executive positions or civil servants who will pay. It will be the four million or five million Canadians who do not have drug plans, those who are self-employed and those generally in lower income brackets. Instead of paying $2 for a prescription drug, they will pay perhaps $10 or $12. Of course that has been well documented by CBC and other groups.
I do not agree with the legislation. I think if the Government had come forward with the kind of legislation the Eastman report recommended, it would have received a lot of support. I am not sure the New Democratic Party would have supported it, but the Government certainly would have received support from our caucus.
The Eastman report stayed on middle ground. It costs about $100 million to create a new pharmaceutical drug. There is a reasonable argument for, say, a four year exclusive patent right and perhaps a special fund for R and D. If the Government had brought forward that kind of legislation, we would have supported it. However, this is just a locked in patent legislation. There is certainly no evidence that the R and D commitment will be kept. Over a 17 year period of exclusive patent rights, the benefits to Canadians compared to the costs are simply not there.
I hope the Government will support this amendment which simply gives a definition of "research" under the Act. I mentioned the importance of the excellent Eastman report which looked at the whole industry. As I indicated, the report stayed in the middle in providing adequate benefit to the drug companies if they actually do original research which creates new drugs which are beneficial to Canadians.
The Minister spent a considerable time justifying his legislation by quoting a poll, which I suppose his caucus paid for and therefore received the answers they wanted. I would point out to Hon. Members of the House the results of the Reid poll taken in January 1987. It asked the question:
As you may know, the Government recently presented legislation which will give drug companies exclusive patent rights to manufacture and sell the drugs they invented for a longer period of time than they have now. Other companies will not be allowed to produce or sell less expensive copies of most drugs for 10 years. Do you yourself support or oppose this proposed legislation?
This survey was conducted on a 1666 sample base across the country. Only 30 per cent supported the position of the Government. 58 per cent opposed it. Twelve per cent were unsure. In Ontario, 54 per cent were opposed and 32 per cent were in favour. In Quebec, 35 per cent supported the legislation and 54 per cent were opposed. However, across the entire country, there was an almost two to one opposition to the legislation.
The amendment put forward by the Hon. Member Cape Breton-East Richmond is important. We are trying to pin down exactly what it is the Government requires in this legislation, so it can provide some written commitment.
April 1, 1987

This legislation does not even mention R and D. This amendment attempts to identify what R and D is, using an existing definition. If we are going to give this exclusive right for 10 or 17 years, and Canadians are going to have to pay $3 or $4 billion in return for only $1.4 billion in R and D, surely we should have a definition included in the legislation so we know where we are going, what the trade off is, and what the benefit is. At least, in our amendment, we have identified exactly what "research and development" is.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-22, and more specifically on the amending motion presented by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Richmond East (Mr. Dingwall).
Mr. Speaker, your decision to let the House debate this motion separately is an indication of its importance. You could have decided to regroup the motion with others as you did for a number of other amendments, but I believe your decision was the right one. I shall, if I may, read the amendment presented by the Liberals, motion No. 2, dated March 5, 1987. The definition of "research"is as follows:
""research" is exploratory and innovative work undertaken on a systematic
basis towards the acquisition of new knowledge in new ways.
New knowledge involves the integration of newly acquired information into
existing hypothesis, the formulation and testing of new hypothesis or the reevaluation of existing observations."
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? How discoveries are made has always been a subject of'debate within the scientific community. Pemac told us that clinical research produces new pharmaceutical products. That is true. However, we must make a distinction between research on changing the colour of pills and research on a new drug that might, for instance, cure AIDS.
In our amendment, "research" is defined partly as "exploratory and innovative work undertaken on a systematic basis towards the acquisition of new knowledge and new ways". If that definition is not clearly indicated in the Act, the multinationals are going to set up their own. And I can guarantee they will not benefit Canadians or job creation in the high technology sector.
Blinded by the promises of the U.S. multinationals, the Minister told us the Bill would create 3,000 jobs. To hear the Minister, one would think all these jobs would be created in the research sector. I suggest we look at the straight facts. As we all know, to do research, scientists first have to do their experiments and testing on animals. That means people to clean the cages, people to take care of the animals at night and adminstrators to run the offices. Do people in the scientific communauty want to do that kind of work? Of course not. Do young graduates fresh out of university want to do that work? Certainly not! What we finally have is not 3,000 jobs in the research sector. If 3,000 jobs are created, nearly a third of
Patent Act
those jobs, 600 or more, will be cage cleaner, janitor and administrator jobs.
Mr. Speaker, it is no surprise the multinational corporations did not convince this Conservative Government to insert into the Act the definition of the term "research". The reason is that those corporations did not want one. It was in their interest not to leave one. Because they succeeded in having the legislation amended between June, 1986 and November, 1986. After failing to have a Bill passed in 1986, the Government came back in November 1986 with a much weaker legislation. Clearly, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) bowed to pressures from President Reagan, the American Congress and the multinational corporations. One of the amendments made to the legislation between June and November dealt with manufacturing of basic ingredients. The June bill would have forced multinationals to manufacture basic ingredients in Canada, or else they were to lose their licenses. The November Bill has completely left out that clause, which means multinationals can go on, and I repeat go on importing ingredients from Puerto Rico or any other Third World nation. Worse still, they will be able to go on overstating the costs of their imports in order to avoid paying taxes.
I sincerely believe that if the term "research" is not defined in the Bill, the multinationals will have a free hand. As an example, some people say that discoveries happen by chance. Others in the scientific community believe that new discoveries stem from clinical manipulation, and others still, because of structured methods.
For all those reasons, the multinationals will have a free hand not to do any scientific research. They could for instance decide to have their significant research done in Switzerland, France, Belgium, England or, worse still, the United States, next door. And those same multinationals could make it a game of changing the colour of their pills in Canada. All this may happen in Canada if the bill includes no definition of the term "research".
I have two reasons to believe that very little research will be done in Canada. First, when the Government dropped the requirement for multinationals to manufacture basic ingredients in Canada, it thereby gave them an opportunity to paralyse all scientific development in that area. Why for example should generic drug manufacturers have to manufacture basic ingredients in Canada if the multinationals can go and buy their stocks in Puerto Rico?
As you see, Mr. Speaker, if the multinationals had been required to manufacture in Canada, we could have developed that side of research and I am convinced that the generic companies would have been more willing to invest.
But the problem is this: Why should generic companies bother investing in and developing a new basic ingredient research industry even if they could reduce by as many as three years the 10 year protection period to the patentee, when major multinationals will continue buying abroad their ingredients? Even if they decided to develop a basic ingredient

research industry, generic companies would find the market closed, because they would be the only users of their own products.
The other reason that leads me to believe that very little medical research will be carried out in Canada stems from the high priority the Americans are giving defence research. My rationale is this. In May and June 1985, I sat on the Liberal Committee which dealt with Star Wars. We travelled everywhere in Canada. We received and heard several briefs. Several scientists and academics explained to us that it is often quite by accident if discoveries made by NASA and other branches of the US Defence Department end up in medical research sections. When asked if they could estimate the cost for defence research and for medical research, they could not give us a clear answer.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, how can anyone imagine that the Americans are going to transfer their medical research to Canada, when we know how closely connected it is to Defence Department research? As I said, they will come to Canada only to change the colour and shape of their pills.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that we, as Liberals, are not against the ten year protection, when the research is fully carried out in Canada with funds such as those from the Terry Fox and Steve Fonyo Foundations. The Ottawa-Carleton Chapter of the Multiple Sclerosis Society also share this view.
In other words, we are prepared to accept changes, but not at any cost. If the Government were serious, it would accept our amendment.

Frankly, I can think of no more appropriate welcome for the President of the United States than the withdrawal of this Bill. The President of the United States should be led to recognize that this country is an independent self-directing country, a country which will take its own course with respect to the pharmaceutical industry, with respect to patent legislation, and not be put into the position where it has to accept certain demands from the United States, as has clearly happened in this case, in order to get some kind of free trade arrangement with that country.
Despite my disappointment, Mr. Speaker, I wish to talk this afternoon about the amendment that is before us, an amendment which attempts to do what is surely very basic to any effort to pass legislation of this kind, that amendment being to define "research".
If, as the Minister suggests, there is going to be this tremendous increase, this upsurge of research that will take place in Canada with respect to pharmaceuticals, surely it is possible, in the Bill which is going to make this happen, to define what "research" will be, thus enabling us to measure it
April 1, 1987

and to assess whether the Minister, in his claims, turns out to be correct or incorrect.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I want to talk a little bit about research. I wish to quote from a book entitled The Economics of Industrial Innovation some of the lessons which that book should have brought to this Government in its thinking about patents and in its thinking about research in pharmaceuticals.
Certainly, pharmaceuticals, as this book points out, represent a research-intensive part of the industrial structure. The figures from the United Kingdom, for instance, indicate that pharmaceuticals, in that country, contribute something in the order of 7 per cent of the net output of firms to research. That compares to a figure of 1.3 per cent for the iron and steel industry, a figure of only 2.1 per cent for machine tools, and a figure of 2.3 per cent for general mechanical engineering.
So certainly we are talking about a research-intensive industry. But the question which must face us is: Is this an industry which this Bill is going to make research-intensive here in Canada?
In the past in Canada, it has not had that reputation. If we take, for instance, the assessment of Dr. Joel Lexchin, a Toronto doctor who has investigated what research has actually been undertaken by the Canadian drug industry, he makes the following point: The little research money that is spent in Canada is divided into three areas. Only 8 per cent goes to basic research, which seeks to discover new concepts of drug therapy or totally new drug products; 36 per cent is used for applied research, which consists of testing potential drugs; and 56 per cent is applied to product development, which effectively is the small changes in dosage or in the reformulation of drugs, creams, or solutions.
So in the past we have not had a drug industry in this country which has given us the kind of research-intensive industry on which we could build exports, jobs, and growth.
Bill C-22 has fallen into the myth of accepting that the research which will give us that new approach, that new thrust toward innovation, will be research which will come from foreign companies being given their way here in our country.
I wish government Members had looked carefully at this book before drafting this legislation. Had they done so, they would have seen the results of Project Sappho in the United Kingdom, a project which attempted to investigate, scientifically, what it was that encouraged success in industry, success in firms with respect to innovation. They would have become aware of the conclusion that there is no systematic evidence that indicates that larger or smaller firms are more or less successful in research and development.
The myth that suggests that it is the large foreign firm that is going to give us our research success is simply not backed up by the research which has been undertaken. In fact, if one goes on from what was not a factor in shaping success or failure to what was a factor, the key points made in this Project Sappho study indicate clearly that what makes for success is direct
Patent Act
knowledge of the market and an understanding of user requirements.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what we are going to get, not from the foreign pharmaceutical multinationals, which simply transfer their drugs to this country, but from building up in this country itself, on the basis of the generic industry, an indigenous powerful and successful Canadian drug industry, an industry which would know the market, which would know user requirements, and which, therefore, would be successful in research and development.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what we are in favour of; that is why we are so strongly opposed to this Bill which has been brought before us.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to say a few words on the proposed legislation and, in particular, on the amendment which is before the House.
I listened very carefully to what the Government has said over the last several months in defence of the legislation to amend Canada's Patent Act insofar as pharmaceutical products are concerned. I think I am fairly accurate in saying that its major defence seems to be, first, the creation of jobs in Canada and, second, the creation of Canadian based research and development on new pharmaceutical products.
In response to statements by the Government, some multinational corporations indicated publicly that they were prepared to make a fairly substantial commitment to research and development in Canada if the legislation were indeed passed.
A couple of things must be said about the legislation. There is nothing in it which requires multinational corporations to follow through with their commitment to increase research and development in Canada. Also, I find it extremely confusing to hear the Government talk about the need to increase research and development expenditures when in fact it has been cutting back on funding for research activity across the country.
Let us look at what multinational corporations have been talking about. The press releases indicate that they are not really talking about increasing expenditures for research and development. They are talking about perhaps putting more money into clinical research in Canada. Anyone who has looked carefully at the difference between the two knows that there is a significant difference. In the research and development activity money is used to develop and find new drugs, whereas clinical research is simply the process of looking at drugs coming on the market as they go through the approval process at the Department of National Health and Welfare.
For example, when Parke-Davis announced increased funding in a press release, it indicated that the money would be used for plant expansion, development of pharmaceutical firms, and the basic study of new drugs. It did not talk about research and development; it talked about clinical research.

April 1, 1987
Patent Act
When the Upjohn company made its announcement of new investment, it spoke about phase two clinical research, establishing a quality control laboratory, expanded office space, and manufacturing facilities.
Before the Minister or any other person in the House starts jumping on the bandwagon and talking about how there will be increased research in Canada, we should start looking closely at what the corporations are talking about. What they are talking about is attempting to pull the wool over the eyes of Canadians on these promises.
A few months ago I was in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia when an announcement was made about a new commitment from multinational companies in respect of additional funds for research and development on Cape Breton Island. The Minister of Health for Nova Scotia had an interesting response to the announcement. He asked, even if the money were made available-and he doubted it very much-under the most charitable circumstances, and even if the legislation went through the House of Commons and the investment was actually made on Cape Breton Island, what would it mean for the people in Cape Breton? It would mean very little, because what they would propose to do is to educate students on Cape Breton Island in certain research and development skills. However, after they had received those skills, they could not apply them in Cape Breton because there are no manufacturing facilities for pharmaceutical products in Cape Breton or in Nova Scotia.
That Minister pointed out quite correctly that the kids would have to leave their communities, families, friends, and close associates and move to either Quebec or Ontario in order to obtain employment in the industry. He said that if the Government were interested in creating jobs in the Atlantic provinces, it should get those companies to invest dollars in creating direct jobs in Nova Scotia where they are badly needed. He did not say that idly.
Professor Eastman, in my view and in the view of many others, has probably conducted the most extensive examination of how multinational corporations work in the pharmaceutical industry, not only in Canada but world-wide. I should like to quote what Professor Eastman said on page 423 of his report:
Canada does not now possess either the scientific manpower or the physical infrastructure that would make it a major world centre for basic pharmaceutical research. Nor in the opinion of the Commission would it be wise for Governments to seek to create such an environment in competition with heavily supported, long established centres in other countries.
That was Professor Eastman's conclusion. What have we heard from generic manufacturers in Canada, those companies which have become quite sophisticated in copying brand name drugs over the years? They have now become so sophisticated that they are at the point where they can now begin their own research and development activity in Canada. However, the legislation will put the brakes on that because it will make it extremely difficult for those wholly owned Canadian companies, which provide jobs for Canadians, to reinvest any profits back into the Canadian economy or to expand job creation in
Canada. Also the legislation will make it very difficult for them to continue to operate in the Canadian interest. Frankly, I find the legislation to be peculiar, to say the least.
The Conservative Government was elected on the promise of jobs, jobs, jobs. However, in the case of an industry which is doing its best in the Canadian corporate sector to create jobs, the Government is introducing legislation which will put that industry's back to the wall. It just does not make sense, any way one looks at it.
Canada's legislation, as it was passed in 1969 and as it has been reviewed by no less than seven commissions, including an all-party House of Commons committee, Professor Eastman, and internal studies by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, has been a good policy for Canadians. As we all know, Professor Eastman pointed out that in 1983 alone Canadian consumers saved something in the area of $211 million as a result of that policy. It is a "made-in-Canada" policy. It is good for Canada and good for Canadians. Quite frankly, the only reason it is being changed is that President Ronald Reagan in the United States does not like it and is demanding on behalf of the multinational industry that it be changed.
I see that my time is up. Thank you very much.

As I read in this week's issue of the Journal des affaires which has been circulated from coast to coast, Mr. Speaker, this legislation is truly fantastic, and no matter what the NDP may say we, as Quebec Members of the Conservative Party, are all for it.
When we consider the total volume of the promised investments, we can look forward to a 60/40 sharing between Ontario and Quebec. And this investment distribution will reflect the research and development manpower within the industry, as represented in the two major Canadian provinces. About 43 companies in Ontario and Quebec are members of the Association, with nearly 600 researchers in Quebec and 40 in Ontario. Although the number of employees may differ today, the proportion remains the same. And even if in 1983, 8,600 employees were recorded in Ontario, compared to 6,300 in Quebec, out of a total 15,500 employees for the whole of Canada. The investment in research and development will

reflect the distribution of researchers, which will favour Quebec, because this is where the greatest concentration is.
On the same subject, Mr. Speaker, the Journal des affaires, which is deservedly famous throughout the world, but especially in Quebec and the rest of Canada, is contemplating that approximately 40 per cent of all investments will be made in Quebec, 40 per cent in Ontario, 40 per cent in the western provinces, and 4 per cent in the Atlantic provinces. I read on. It says that it will create directly 3,000 new jobs in the industry. That is quite good for Quebec, Mr. Speaker. But there is one thing I should like to warn the House about, and it is the cost of medicine. Several people in my region of Abitibi have told me that the NDP constantly infer that the costs will increase. They keep saying that promises are always fine, but that they are quickly forgotten. To make sure that the companies will fulfill their promises and will not pass on their research costs to consumers through unjustified increases in the price of medicine, the Bill provides for a control mechanism. I mean, there will be a monitoring agency.
Mr. Speaker, that is truly what our party, our Government is doing for Quebec and the rest of Canada. We are going to monitor the prices right away. That will be a very good Bill and senior citizens . . . Well, the prices on these drugs will not increase anyway.

Mr. Speaker, since it is nearly six o'clock, perhaps you could call it six o'clock, and I could start my speech tomorrow. Or perhaps I could start with the preliminaries.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. In the few minutes or few seconds remaining, I would like to pay special tribute to the Hon. Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) who finally set the record straight on the whole NDP situation-these radical leftwingers who are so terribly pleased with themselves and who claim they represent the people of Quebec and French Canadians in general. Today, we see just what kind of representation they are giving them. Their insincerity is flagrant. As for the Conservatives opposite, Mr. Speaker, they are the people who introduced this Bill. They did what they usually do: they caved in to the multinationals and they got down on their knees before President Reagan, which was predictable of the Conservative Party.
